misconception_pool.misconception: Unplugging a television or microwave from the wall outlet immediately removes all electrical shock hazards inside the casing.
misconception_pool.fact: High-voltage capacitors retain lethal electrical charges long after unplugging and must never be touched during an inspection.

misconception_pool.misconception: Mechanical engineers alone design household appliances without input from electrical, materials, or manufacturing engineers.
misconception_pool.fact: Appliance creation requires materials engineers for heat plastics, electrical engineers for circuits, and manufacturing teams.

misconception_pool.misconception: Plastic gears inside a cordless drill or kitchen mixer are chosen only to lower production cost rather than for engineering reasons.
misconception_pool.fact: Engineers often specify nylon sacrificial gears to shear safely under a jam and protect the expensive electric motor from burning out.

misconception_pool.misconception: Investigating how a sealed lithium-ion battery pack works requires prying open the metal cell pouch with a flathead screwdriver.
misconception_pool.fact: Puncturing a lithium-ion cell triggers thermal runaway and fire, so battery subsystems must be studied only from external labels.

pamphlet_excerpts: Problem Definition: Define operational constraints, target users, functional requirements, and performance objectives before sketching.
Trade Studies: Compare competing prototype concepts against cost, weight, durability, and ease of manufacturing.
Subsystem Integration: Ensure mechanical linkages, electrical power feeds, and user control interfaces fit together.
Iterative Testing: Subject physical prototypes to realistic stress testing to expose unexpected mechanical failure modes.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Requirements Definition: Establish specific user needs, dimensional constraints, and operational goals for the device.
Step 2 - Conceptual Ideation: Generate multiple design sketches evaluating different mechanical linkages and structural material choices.
Step 3 - Prototype Construction: Build a working model utilizing readily available shop materials and hand tools.
Step 4 - Performance Validation: Test the prototype under field conditions and record required design modifications systematically.

misconception_pool.misconception: Engineering design is a linear sequence where the initial drawing is constructed directly without changes.
misconception_pool.fact: Systems engineering relies on cyclical iteration where testing reveals flaws that force design revisions.

misconception_pool.misconception: Systems engineering means building the first idea that comes to mind and writing down the specifications after it is finished.
misconception_pool.fact: Systems engineering starts by defining user needs and measurable constraints, then compares alternatives before building a prototype.

misconception_pool.misconception: A prototype test that bends, jams, or falls short of the target metric proves that the systems engineering process has failed.
misconception_pool.fact: Prototype test failures provide essential feedback data that guides the next design iteration to strengthen weak interfaces.

misconception_pool.misconception: Optimizing every single component for maximum strength and weight always produces the best overall patrol equipment system.
misconception_pool.fact: Overbuilding individual parts can make a camp system too heavy to carry; systems engineering balances interfaces across the whole unit.

misconception_pool.misconception: Sketching a rough picture without dimensions, material callouts, or bill of materials is sufficient for an engineering design plan.
misconception_pool.fact: A buildable engineering design requires dimensioned drawings, tolerances, and a material list so another person can reproduce it.

requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Transforming Motion. Using common materials or a construction set, make a simple model that will demonstrate motion. Explain how the model uses basic mechanical elements like levers and inclined planes to demonstrate motion. Describe an example where this mechanism is used in a real product. (b) Using Electricity. Make a list of 10 electrical appliances in your home. Find out approximately how much electricity each uses in one month. Learn how to find out the amount and cost of electricity used in your home during periods of light and heavy use. List five ways to conserve electricity. (c) Understanding Electronics. Using an electronic device such as a smartphone or tablet computer, find out how sound, video, text or images travel from one location to another. Explain how the device was designed for ease of use, function, and durability. (d) Using Materials. Do experiments to show the differences in strength and heat conductivity in wood, metal, and plastic. Discuss with your counselor what you have learned. (e) Converting Energy. Do an experiment to show how mechanical, heat, chemical, solar, and/or electrical energy may be converted from one or more types of energy to another. Explain your results. Describe to your counselor what energy is and how energy is converted and used in your surroundings. (f) Moving People. Find out the different ways people in your community get to work. Make a study of traffic flow (number of vehicles and relative speed) in both heavy and light traffic periods. Discuss with your counselor what might be improved to make it easier for people in your community to get where they need to go. (g) Building an Engineering Project. Enter a project in a science or engineering fair or similar competition. (This requirement may be met by participation on an engineering competition project team.) Discuss with your counselor what your project demonstrates, the kinds of questions visitors to the fair asked you, and how well you were able to answer their questions.
